chapter: Piano craft and the New York school
title: Teddy Wilson and the era of amplified recording
summary: Teddy Wilson, whom Ramirez replaced with Bryant, benefitted from recording technology and microphones, like Basie.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Well, after being exposed to and developing a friendship with Tatum, would you say your next influence, or your next pianistic encounter would be with Teddy Wilson?
Yeah, I would say so, especially for band and all combo work. His style was very popular.
You took his place with Willie Bryant.
And that's where you met him?
Well, I'd met him before that, when he first came here with Benny Carter.

Well, his style was more of a pianistic approach, ...(?)... Earl Hines, and he liked...I would say he listened to Tatum, played some runs like Art Tatum. But the unique thing, he was very... I don't know, he was very tuned to small combos -- you know, out from bands. But at that time, of course, he enjoyed the fact that with the technology of reproduction, amplification and things like that, you could hear all his subtle things much more clearly, you know, than you could in the old days. Remember, even singers in the old days used megaphones, and they could be heard up to a point. But as I said, Teddy enjoyed an era, and Count Basie I would say too enjoyed an era where through recording... You could hear what they were playing, you know, because the reproduction...
They come into the picture about the same time, really, don't they, as far as the public was concerned.
